lesson.title: Incident drills: practise before it happens
lesson.subtitle: A thirty-minute tabletop exercise for your staff

video.title: Incident drills: practise before it happens
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher and the school's cyber lead (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Early morning. Salma answers her phone at her kitchen table; on a laptop beside her, the school's page shows a post with a laptop picture and a price tag.
scenes.animation: Phone rings with a shake; the post slides into view.
scenes.narration: At seven in the morning, a parent called me. “Why is the school page selling cheap laptops?” Our page had been taken over in the night, and nobody knew who should do what.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and the cyber track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot; title slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Incident drills: practise before it happens
scenes.narration: Today: how to run a thirty-minute incident drill, so your school knows what to do before it happens.

scenes.visual: Teachers around a staffroom table with paper and tea. Salma reads from a card; three numbered cards are turned over one at a time.
scenes.animation: Cards flip in turn; a notebook fills with lines.
scenes.narration: A tabletop drill is a story your staff work through around a table, with no computers needed. You tell it in three short updates, one after another. After each one, the team says what they would do, and someone writes it down.

scenes.visual: Four role cards are handed round the table, each with an icon: a compass for the lead, a megaphone, a spanner, a notebook.
scenes.animation: Cards slide to each seat in turn.
scenes.narration: Give out four roles. The incident lead decides. The communications lead is the only voice to parents. The technical helper deals with accounts and devices. And the record keeper writes down what happened, and when.

scenes.visual: Three scenario cards fan out: a school page with a fake fee offer, a locked office screen with a calendar showing exams, a chat bubble asking parents for money.
scenes.animation: Cards fan out one by one.
scenes.on_screen_text: Pick a story that could happen
scenes.narration: Pick a story that could really happen to you. The school page taken over, posting fake fee offers. Ransomware on the office computer two days before exams. Or a teacher’s WhatsApp taken over, asking parents for money.

scenes.visual: A fire drill in the schoolyard: pupils line up; a teacher finds a door blocked by chairs and moves them.
scenes.animation: Pupils file out; the blocked door is cleared.
scenes.narration: It’s like a fire drill. Nobody waits for a real fire to find out the exit is blocked. A cyber drill finds the blocked exits: the missing password, the backup nobody can find, the phone number nobody has.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph at the drill table, holding up the second update card. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Character slides in; answer cards drop with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! In our drill, the page is still posting scam links, and parents are calling every teacher. Who should answer them?

scenes.visual: The communications lead card gets a blue check badge. A short message appears in the official parents' group; teachers point callers to it.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; the message slides up line by line.
scenes.narration: The communications lead, with one short message on a channel parents already trust. “Our page was taken over. Don’t pay anything it asks for. We’ll update you by five.” Everyone else points parents to that message.

scenes.visual: Salma's drill notes: a recovery email with a question mark, a USB drive with a question mark, and a printed card of phone numbers pinned inside a cupboard door.
scenes.animation: Each item appears with a question mark that turns into a tick.
scenes.narration: Drills test the boring things that save you. Can you find the page’s recovery email? Where is last week’s backup? And if the internet is down, is there a paper card with the key phone numbers?

scenes.visual: After the drill: three lessons written on the board; a second admin is added to the page; then staff try a short scam quiz on paper, with no names on the sheets.
scenes.animation: Lines write on; a second admin badge appears; quiz sheets slide in.
scenes.narration: When the drill ends, write down three lessons. Change one thing for each: the contact card, a second admin for the page, where the backup lives. Then finish with a quick spot-the-scam round, with everyone’s agreement and no names on the scores.

scenes.visual: Salma at the head of the table. Two answer cards bounce in: a pointing finger (blame) and an open hand (no blame).
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. In our story, a teacher clicked a fake link first. Should the drill end by finding someone to blame?

scenes.visual: The open-hand card gets the check badge. Four summary cards line up.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.narration: No: people who fear blame hide mistakes, and hidden mistakes grow. Remember: a real story in three updates, four roles, one voice to parents, and real changes afterwards.

scenes.visual: Salma knocks on the head teacher's door holding a folder with one scenario card and four role cards.
scenes.animation: Door opens; the head teacher nods and writes in a diary.
scenes.narration: Try it at school tomorrow: ask your head teacher for thirty minutes of the next staff meeting. Bring one scenario on paper, and four role cards.

checkpoints.prompt: During the drill, parents are calling every teacher about the scam posts. Who should answer them?

options.text: Every teacher who gets a call, in their own words
The communications lead, with one message on an official channel
Nobody, until the page is fixed

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: one voice and one message, on a channel parents already trust.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: many voices give mixed messages, and silence lets the scam spread. One named person warns parents on an official channel.

checkpoints.prompt: In the drill story, a teacher clicked a fake link first. Should the drill end by finding someone to blame?

options.text: Yes: someone has to answer for it
No: blame stops people reporting early

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: when people fear blame they hide mistakes, and every hour hidden makes an incident worse.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: blame teaches people to hide mistakes. A drill looks for weak steps, not for culprits.
